extraction_text: Bhishma narrated an ancient legend about sages visiting pilgrimage sites and making vows.
The sages gathered at Prabhasa in the west and decided to visit all sacred places on earth.
The sages appointed Indra (also called Shakra or Hundred-Sacrifices) as their leader for the pilgrimage.
The sages traveled across the earth and arrived at the sacred Gautami River during the full moon of Magha month.
After purifying themselves at other sacred sites, they reached the holy Brahma Lake where gods frequent.
The sages entered the water and began collecting lotus flowers and roots.
Agastya discovered his pile of lotus flowers had disappeared from the shore.
Agastya accused the other sages of stealing his lotus flowers and demanded their return.
Agastya declared he would leave for the future world and never return before witnessing various signs of moral decline.

extraction_text: Various sages and kings pronounce curses on whoever takes the lotus.
Indra (千眼天王/天帝释/摩珂梵) observes the curses and is pleased.
Indra addresses the angry Sage Agastya (投山仙人) and presents his own view.
Indra pronounces his own conditions for whoever takes the lotus, involving virtuous acts and ultimate reward.
The narrative is recounted by Bhishma (毗湿摩) to the Kuru king (俱卢族国王).
Indra took the lotus flowers from the ascetic, claiming it was to hear people's discourse on dharma.
Atri demanded the return of his lotus flowers, citing the principle of returning what is taken.
Indra explained his actions were not driven by greed but by a desire to understand dharma, and returned the lotus flowers.
Atri, initially angry, became happy after retrieving his lotus flowers.
Yudhishthira asked Bhishma about the origin and purpose of the custom of giving umbrellas and shoes during ancestral rites and other auspicious occasions.

extraction_text: Bhishma agreed to explain the origin, prevalence, and significance of the custom of giving umbrellas and shoes.
Bhishma began narrating an ancient conversation between Sage Agastya and the Sun God about the custom.
Agastya practiced archery continuously while his wife Renuka collected and returned his arrows.
During the month when the sun reaches the constellations of Anuradha and Jyeshtha, at noon, Jamadagni ran out of arrows and asked Renuka to retrieve them.
Renuka went to collect the arrows but stopped under a tree's shade because the intense sun caused her head and feet pain.
Renuka, fearing her husband's curse, overcame her hesitation and continued to collect the arrows, then returned to Jamadagni.
Jamadagni angrily questioned Renuka about the delay.
Renuka explained she took shelter under a tree due to the sun's intense heat causing her pain.
Jamadagni declared he would shoot down the sun with his arrows for causing Renuka's suffering.
Jamadagni gathered arrows, strung his divine bow, and aimed at the moving sun.
Surya (Sun God) disguised as a Brahmin appeared before Jamadagni and questioned his anger.
Surya explained the sun's essential role in the water cycle, rainfall, food production, and sustaining all life and human activities.
Surya urged Jamadagni to understand these facts and reconsider shooting down the sun.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma whether the sage Agastya changed his attitude after the Sun God's entreaty.
